I.         Introduction

           4K Land and Cattle Company (“4K Land”) files these Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”) issued by the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) on August 20, 2026,

pursuant to 16 Texas Administrative Code § 22.261.

           4K Land owns approximately 100,000 acres of land in Mason, McCulloch, and San Saba

Counties, Texas (the “4K Ranch”), a diversified, actively managed operation encompassing

commercial cattle production, hay and forage production, agricultural farming, comprehensive

wildlife management, hunting leases and guided hunts, ecotourism, and equestrian activities. 1

Links M12, M11, K52, and K51, would inflict substantial, permanent, and unmitigable harm on

the 4K Ranch. 2

           4K Land supports the ALJs’ recommendation that the Application for a Certificate of

Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) be denied. 3 However, should the Commission reject the

denial recommendation and proceed to approve the Application, 4K Land takes exception to the

ALJs’ contingent routing recommendation of Route 894, and to specific findings of fact and

conclusions of law that fail to account for the record evidence concerning:

                  (1) the absence of a defensible routing methodology;

                  (2) the lack of any visual resource analysis;

                  (3) the substantial harm Route 894 would inflict on the 4K Ranch;

                  (4) the superiority of Northern Corridor alternatives; and

                  (5) the terrain and environmental deficiencies of the Route 894 corridor.

  each individual project within the plan satisfies the statutory criteria for a CCN. 7

 VIII.         Routing Criteria (Issues 8-10)

               Should the Commission reject the ALJs’ denial recommendation and proceed to approve

   the Application, 4K Land takes exception to the ALJs’ contingent recommendation of Route 894.

   The record evidence, properly weighed, demonstrates that Route 894 is not the route that best

   meets the statutory and regulatory criteria, and that Northern Corridor alternatives—particularly

   Routes 410, 416, 392, and related routes—are superior under every recognized routing

   methodology in the record.


               B. Intervenor Concerns Regarding Routing Methodology

               4K Land excepts to the PFD and FOF 67, which finds that the Application provided

   adequate routes. 14 The PFD also provided the contingent recommendation of Route 894. 15

               The PFD accepts Route 894 as the best route without addressing Applicants’ failure to file

   a documented routing methodology. Yet the record is unequivocal: what Applicants filed is not a

   methodology. 16 A methodology is the governing framework—the principles, sequence, and

   documented rationale that tell any subsequent reviewer how the work was done and whether it can

   be reproduced. 17 What Applicants filed are methods—buffer operations, weighted overlays, least-

   cost path calculations—without the disciplining framework that a methodology provides. 18

               The Applicants’ own routing witnesses acknowledged that the EPRI-GTC standard (EPRI

   Report No. 1013080, the Overhead Electric Transmission Line Siting Methodology) exists and

           This admission is fatal. A routing analysis whose weights are acknowledged to be

unconstrained cannot demonstrate that the resulting routes best meet the Commission’s routing

criteria, because the criteria themselves are operationalized in the weights. 21 Under Mr. Scott’s

multi-criteria weighted-suitability analysis (Exhibit JS-3), Route 894 ranks 83rd of 122 routes;

Northern Corridor Routes 410 and 416 tie for first; Route 392 ranks third. 22

           Route 894 supporters offered no independent routing methodology, relying instead on

Applicants’ metrics. 23 The PFD errs by crediting the output of an undisciplined process without

addressing whether that process can yield a defensible result.

           Accordingly, the Commission should reject FOF 67 to the extent it implies Applicants filed

a defensible routing methodology, and should modify FOF 223 and related findings to no longer

identify Route 894 as the route that best addresses the statutory and regulatory criteria, as further

detailed below.

Applicants’ study area was drawn before—not derived from—proper base terrain analysis.

             Based on the testimony of 4K Land witness Mr. Scott, the four-factor exploration envelope

that a standards-compliant process (EPRI-GTC) would generate is approximately 2.6 times the

geographic extent of the filed study area. 24 The northern portion of that proper exploration

envelope contains corridors identified through standards-compliant analysis that were excluded

before analysis began. 25 Applicants’ failure to examine this broader geography means that the filed

routes may not include corridors that would better satisfy the statutory criteria.

            Within the constrained study area Applicants did examine, route differentiation is nominal:

the cost range spans approximately 13% of the median; Route 894 sits only 2.7% above the cost

floor; 85 habitable structures is only 5 more than the minimum of 80. 26 These narrow margins

indicate that the study area itself—not the underlying terrain—is driving route outcomes.

            The Commission should find that the study area derivation is not documented or defensible,

and that the routing recommendation cannot be credited absent a study area derived from base

terrain analysis.

Characterization, Hydrologic Characterization, Critical Ecological Features, and People, Places &

Experiences—each aligned to the enumerated statutory factors and independently computed,

           The PFD’s reliance on former Chairman Smitherman’s statement that route selection is

“not a math question” and former Commissioner McAdams’s characterization of scoring as “in

among enumerated factors is a set of weights—whether or not anyone writes them down. Former

Chairman Smitherman’s own testimony confirms this: the statute provides “a subjective balancing

of factors” in which, once specific facts are established, particular concerns “need to be weighted

heavily.” 32 Mr. Scott’s analysis performs and documents that balancing. The “eye of the beholder”

characterization describes the Applicants’ undisclosed process—from the same data, Applicants

selected Route 894, Staff selected Route 487, and Staff’s witness agreed another qualified engineer

could reasonably reach a different conclusion. 33 This does not describe Mr. Scott’s transparent,

reproducible, disclosed analysis.

            C. Community Values

           4K Land excepts to the PFD’s FOF 176, which conclusorily states that “Route 894

adequately addresses the expressed community values.” 34 This finding fails to engage with the

record evidence demonstrating that the community values expressed throughout the study area—

preservation of working ranches, protection of the Hill Country landscape, avoidance of new

industrial corridors through undisturbed terrain, and conservation of scenic and ecological

resources—weigh against Route 894 and in favor of Northern Corridor alternatives. PURA §

37.056(c)(4)(A) requires the Commission to consider community values, which the Commission

has defined as “a shared appreciation of an area or other mutual resource by a national, regional,

or local community.” 35 The record contains extensive testimony from landowners, wildlife

management associations, and conservation organizations documenting the community’s values

in the Route 894 corridor. Mr. King testified that the 4K Ranch’s approximately 100,000 acres

support a multigenerational stewardship program, wildlife management under TPWD’s Managed

Lands Deer Program, and ecotourism—activities that depend on the undisturbed character of the

land. 36 The Panther Creek Wildlife Management Association, comprising approximately 100

members and 48 contiguous properties managed in coordination with TPWD, testified that Link

G51 (used by Route 894) would cut through its management area—a direct indication of

community values. 37 Yet the PFD’s contingent routing recommendation does not address this

evidence or explain how Route 894 “adequately addresses” these community values when it would

           The PFD’s treatment of community values also fails to account for Commission precedent.

In Docket No. 38290 (the Palo Duro Canyon case), the Commission selected a route that was

approximately 40% longer, 22% more expensive, and impacted more habitable structures in order

to protect community values associated with an iconic Texas landscape—even though the rejected

routes did not directly encroach on the state park. 38 The Commission reasoned that the “strength

of the community values against placing a line across Palo Duro Canyon” outweighed the routes’

advantages on cost, length, and habitable structures. 39 Former PUC Chairman Smitherman

confirmed that a holistic assessment of community values—not a simple habitable-structure

count—is what PURA requires. 40 The same principle applies here: the community values

documented in the record—working ranches, wildlife conservation, Hill Country scenic character,

and the absence of existing industrial infrastructure—favor Northern Corridor alternatives that

follow existing civic and highway corridors rather than Route 894’s traverse through undisturbed

ranchland. The Commission should modify FOF 176 to find that Route 894 does not adequately

address community values, given the unrebutted record evidence of the affected community’s

shared appreciation for the landscape, conservation, and land stewardship that Route 894 would

permanently impair.

           E. Aesthetic and Historic Values

           4K Land excepts to FOF 197, which states that Route 894 “minimizes impacts to aesthetic

values to a reasonable extent [. . .] .” 53

           The record contains no visual resource analysis under any recognized methodology.

Applicants admitted they “did not perform a resource management analysis, viewshed modeling

analysis, or visual contrast rating analysis.” 54 Staff witness Poole confirmed no Visual Resource

Management (“VRM”) analysis exists in the record and agreed it would be useful. 55

           Mr. Scott filed the only VRM analysis in this record (Exhibit JS-3), applying the Bureau

zone count is not a visual resource analysis. 57 It measures residential proximity, not visual contrast,

not the magnitude of landscape alteration, and not the scenic quality of the affected viewshed.

           F. Environmental Integrity; Terrain Suitability

           The PFD does not address terrain suitability, construction accessibility, or soil stability

along Route 894. This is significant in the context of Route 894—which is known for its difficult

terrain—because the Applicants confirmed they conducted no physical site investigation of the

proposed right-of-way prior to filing. 58 Mr. King testified that the Route 894 corridor consists of

rougher terrain with bluffs and rocks where “a road cannot be reasonably constructed.” 59 The

terrain differences between corridors are not captured in Applicants’ desktop metrics. 60

           This testimony was unrebutted. No Route 894 supporter addressed terrain suitability or

construction accessibility. The Commission cannot select a route without considering whether it

can be practically constructed and maintained, particularly when the record identifies specific

terrain obstacles that would increase construction difficulty, environmental disturbance, and long-

term maintenance costs.

            The Commission should add findings reflecting the unrebutted terrain evidence and should

conclude that Route 894’s terrain deficiencies weigh against its selection.

           PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D) names environmental integrity as a distinct factor—separate from

the species, water, and vegetation resources catalogued elsewhere in the record. Naming

environmental integrity as its own factor means the Legislature required an assessment of

integrity—the degree to which a landscape retains its ecological structure, hydrologic function,

and biological composition—not a second inventory of resources. The Environmental Assessment

supplies an inventory of parts (stream crossings, riparian miles, habitat acres) and offers it as an

assessment of the whole. The proof that it is only an inventory is in the Applicants’ own conduct:

Halff removed Links K3, J2, J6, and J5 after the public meetings “due to significant environmental

impacts,” and Mr. Marusak testified “there was no specific boundary to those environmental

concerns.” 61 Environmental harm without a boundary is the signature of a systems effect—yet the

nearest filed links on Route 894 were retained and found “unlikely” to significantly affect

environmental integrity. 62 Mr. Scott’s synthesis analysis—the only analysis in this record that

operates at the level of environmental integrity—demonstrates that Route 894 ranks in the bottom

third of 122 routes on both environmental surfaces: 76th on Critical Ecological Features and 83rd

on the Hydrologic Characterization Index, while Route 392 ranks 7th and 2nd. 63 These surfaces

were placed in the record and drew no competing model and no rebuttal—the evidence was

uncontroverted.
